transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, thank you. Um, so I'm here because... well, it's mostly work stuff. I work at a meat processing plant, which I know sounds kind of intense, especially since I just finished my bachelor's degree, but it's what I'm doing right now. And the thing is, I'm really struggling with, like, actually completing my daily duties. 

What really brings me in is that I keep starting the sanitation steps, the batch logs, or the end-of-line paperwork, and I somehow always leave out the last parts. 

And it's not like I don't care! I know my job absolutely depends on finishing them correctly. Like, with the sanitation steps, that's a huge deal for food safety, obviously. You can't just skip the end. And the batch logs—if an inspector comes in and sees a log isn't finished, it's a massive problem for the whole plant. I know this. I tell myself every single morning, "Just finish the whole form, just do every single step." I get my clipboard, I start going down the checklist, I'm doing great, but then... it's like my brain just decides the task is over before it actually is. 

I'll get to the end of my shift, and my supervisor is pulling me aside again because I missed the last three boxes on the paperwork, or I did the final rinse but didn't actually document the temperature check at the very end. It's so frustrating because I'm trying so hard, and I just don't understand why I can't finish the very last step of a thing I've already put 90 percent of the work into, you know? It's really putting my job on the line, and I'm just constantly terrified I'm going to get fired over a few blank boxes on a form I was literally holding in my hand.
Outside of work, do you find yourself forgetting to finish tasks or missing steps in routine activities, like paying bills, preparing meals, or keeping track of personal items?

Um, no, not really. Honestly, outside of work, I don't really have that same issue. Like, with paying bills, I don't have a problem getting to the end of the process. I just go online, put in the numbers, and hit submit. It's not like the batch logs where there are all these tiny little steps and boxes that just stretch on and on, you know? And with meals, well, I live alone, so I usually just make something super simple, like a sandwich or mac and cheese, or I just grab something on the way home because I'm so exhausted from the plant. There aren't really a lot of steps to miss there. 

And my personal items, like my keys and my phone, I'm actually pretty good about those. I have this little bowl right by the front door, and the second I walk in, I drop my keys in there. I've been doing it since I moved into this apartment because my mom always used to get onto me about losing my keys when I was in high school, so I made it a strict rule for myself. And my phone is basically glued to my hand anyway, so I don't really lose that either. 

It really is just at work. It's like, I cross the threshold of the plant, put on my gear, and my brain just decides it can't handle finishing a checklist. It's so weird because I know I'm capable of finishing things. I mean, I finished my degree, right? You can't just skip the last page of a term paper and graduate. So I know I can do it, which is why it's so incredibly frustrating that I can't just check the last three boxes on a sanitation log. It's just... it's like a block, but only when I'm on the clock. So, yeah, no, at home, I don't really notice that happening at all.

When you're at home, do you ever find yourself losing focus or forgetting the final steps of something, even if it's small or doesn't feel important—like forgetting to close the microwave door after using it, or leaving a glass of water on the counter because you were distracted?

I mean, no, not really. Like I said, it's really just the work stuff that's the problem. I don't leave the microwave door open, because... well, honestly, I don't use the microwave that much anyway, but when I do, I close it. It's just a habit, you know? You open it, you put the food in, you close it, you hit the buttons. I don't really get distracted in the middle of that because it's all right there in front of me and it takes like two seconds. 

And leaving a glass of water on the counter... I don't think so. I usually have a specific water bottle I carry around, this big insulated one I got as a graduation gift, actually. It's bright blue, so it's hard to miss. I take it with me to the couch or my bedside table, and I just kind of keep it with me. I don't really pour glasses of water and just leave them sitting around. I guess maybe sometimes I might leave a mug in the sink instead of putting it straight in the dishwasher, but that's more because I'm just so tired after standing on the line at the plant for eight hours, not because I forgot I was doing it or got distracted. 

It really is just this weird thing at work with the logs and the sanitation steps. It's like my brain just shuts off right at the finish line, but only when I have a clipboard in my hand. At home, I'm just doing my normal routine, and it's fine. I don't have these weird blank spots where I just abandon a task right before it's done. I really wish I could figure out why it's only happening at the plant, because it's making me look so incompetent, and I know I'm not. I just... I don't get it. But yeah, no, at home, I'm not leaving doors open or forgetting things like that.

Do you ever find yourself struggling to finish steps in tasks outside of work when they involve structured routines or checklists, like following a detailed recipe, assembling furniture from a kit, or filling out forms for personal reasons?

Well, I mean... if I really think about it, I guess the answer is that I just don't really do those kinds of things at home? Like, with detailed recipes—I mentioned earlier that I just make really simple stuff because I'm so exhausted. I'm not pulling out a cookbook and following a twelve-step recipe for dinner. I'm just boiling pasta or making a sandwich. So there's no checklist to mess up there, you know? 

And assembling furniture... when I moved into my apartment after graduation, my parents actually helped me move, and my dad put the TV stand together because he loves doing that stuff. The rest of my furniture I just bought used off Facebook Marketplace, so it was already assembled by whoever owned it before me. So I haven't actually tried to follow an assembly kit in... well, I honestly can't even remember the last time I did that. And personal forms? I mean, what forms do I really fill out outside of work? Maybe the intake paperwork for this clinic, but that's about it. My life outside the plant is just pretty unstructured, honestly. I try to keep it that way because work is just so rigid and demanding.

But see, that's exactly why this is so stressful, and it's really what brings me in today. It always comes back to the plant. It’s the fact that I keep starting those sanitation steps, or the batch logs, or the end-of-line paperwork, and I just... I somehow always leave out the last parts. I know we keep talking about it, but it's just dominating my life right now. I know my job depends on finishing them correctly. I know the stakes! The inspectors do not care if you were tired, they only care if the box is checked and the temperature is logged. And yet, I still leave those last sections blank. I just don't understand how I can be so painfully aware of how important it is, and still just... fail to follow through right at the very end of the page. It’s like I hit an invisible wall right before the signature line. So, yeah, I don't really have those structured checklists at home to mess up, but at work, I can't avoid them, and it's driving me completely crazy.
Do you find it hard to start tasks, especially ones that require focus or effort, even if you know they’re important?

Oh, my gosh, yes. That... that is actually a huge issue for me, and again, it really comes up at the plant all the time. We have all these ongoing training things we have to do, and I will literally put off the certification modules and, honestly, any long procedure reading they give us, until the absolute last possible minute. I'm talking, like, my supervisor is coming up to me on the floor saying I'll be locked out of the timekeeping system if I don't finish it by the end of my shift. 

I know how important it is. I mean, it's food safety, it's OSHA regulations, it's USDA guidelines for poultry processing—it's not stuff you can just brush off. But just the mere thought of having to go into the back office, sit down at one of those slow computer terminals, and force myself to read through fifty slides of compliance updates... it's just overwhelming. Sitting there trying to absorb all those rules feels almost physically exhausting. Like, my body literally feels heavy and drained before I even click the first slide. 

I will find a million other things to do first just to avoid starting it. I’ll offer to go scrub down the sanitizing stations again, or I’ll volunteer to go restock the hairnets and the heavy-duty gloves in the supply closet, which isn't even my job, just so I don't have to sit there and force my brain to focus on those modules. Because when I do finally sit down, it’s like trying to wade through wet cement, you know? Every sentence is just so dry, and there are so many acronyms, and I just know I'm going to have to read the same paragraph three times just to get it to stick. So I just avoid it. I completely avoid starting it until the panic of getting written up finally forces me into the chair. And it's so frustrating because if I just did it the day they assigned it, it would be over with, but I just... I can't. The mental block to just start it is just huge.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, even outside of work?

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I'm stressed, obviously, because of everything we've been talking about with the logs and the write-ups, but I don't feel... sad? Or hopeless. Like, I don't sit around crying or feeling like my life is falling apart. 

And I definitely haven't lost interest in the things I like to do. I mean, I still love hanging out with my friends from college—we have this group chat and we still try to do trivia night on Thursdays at this place downtown, and I still really look forward to that every week. Sometimes I'm just physically exhausted, though, because standing on the concrete floor at the poultry plant all day, in those heavy rubber boots, in a room that's kept at like 40 degrees... it just drains you completely. So if I skip trivia, it's literally just because my feet are throbbing and my back aches and I just desperately need a hot shower, not because I don't care about going anymore. I still really want to go. I still love reading, I still enjoy going to the farmer's market on the weekends... it's just the physical tiredness from the line that gets in the way sometimes. 

But mentally? Emotionally? I'm fine. I'm just so, so frustrated with myself about the work stuff. That's the only thing bringing my mood down, just this constant, nagging anxiety that my supervisor is going to pull me into the back office again because I left another temperature check blank on the sanitation sheet. It's not a general dark cloud over my whole life, you know? It's just this one very specific, very maddening problem at the plant that I can't seem to fix, no matter how hard I try or how much I tell myself to pay attention. So, yeah, no depression or anything like that. Just... extreme annoyance at my own brain for messing up these clipboards.

Looking back, did you have similar issues with finishing tasks or staying focused when you were in school, like forgetting to turn in assignments, not completing tests, or struggling to follow through on instructions?

Oh, wow, yeah. It's funny you ask that, because... well, yes, absolutely. Actually, my mom is one of those people who keeps literally everything, like every single scrap of paper from my childhood, and she still has all my old elementary school report cards in this big plastic storage bin at her house. 

We were actually looking at them not that long ago, and my fourth-grade ones—I think it was fourth grade, yeah, because we had just switched to having different teachers for different subjects—anyway, the comments in the margins are just... it's almost exactly what I'm doing now at the plant, just the kid version of it. Every single grading period, the teacher wrote that I was a really bright student, that I had a lot of potential, but that I needed constant, and I mean *constant*, reminders to actually finish my classwork and turn in my homework. 

And the thing is, I remember—I really vividly remember this feeling—I wasn't confused by the material at all. I understood the math lessons, I understood the reading, I got what they were teaching us. But when it came time to actually do the worksheet or follow the project instructions, I would just miss these huge chunks of what we were supposed to do. Like, I’d completely skip the back page, or I’d do the first three steps and then just sort of trail off and start drawing on my folder. It was like, if the teacher was standing right next to my desk, you know, hovering over me or tapping my paper, I could do it. I needed her to literally stay close to me to keep me on track. But the second she walked away to help someone else, my brain would just drift, and I’d miss the second half of the instructions entirely. 

And it's just so frustrating to think about, because I'd always do the homework, or at least start it, but then it would just disappear into the black hole of my backpack and I'd forget to hand it in. People always told me, "You're so smart, if you just applied yourself and paid attention," but I *was* trying! Just like I'm trying with the sanitation logs now! It's like this exact same pattern of just... almost getting there, but leaving the final pieces undone unless someone is standing right over my shoulder watching me do it. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing, it just has much worse consequences now than missing recess did back then.

I remember understanding the lessons but missing chunks of instructions unless the teacher stayed close to me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the history of symptoms during childhood/school years, which corresponds to the requirement of onset prior to age 12.

patient.answer:
Oh, wow, yeah. It's funny you ask that, because... well, yes, absolutely. Actually, my mom is one of those people who keeps literally everything, like every single scrap of paper from my childhood, and she still has all my old elementary school report cards in this big plastic storage bin at her house. 

We were actually looking at them not that long ago, and my fourth-grade ones—I think it was fourth grade, yeah, because we had just switched to having different teachers for different subjects—anyway, the comments in the margins are just... it's almost exactly what I'm doing now at the plant, just the kid version of it. Every single grading period, the teacher wrote that I was a really bright student, that I had a lot of potential, but that I needed constant, and I mean *constant*, reminders to actually finish my classwork and turn in my homework. 

And the thing is, I remember—I really vividly remember this feeling—I wasn't confused by the material at all. I understood the math lessons, I understood the reading, I got what they were teaching us. But when it came time to actually do the worksheet or follow the project instructions, I would just miss these huge chunks of what we were supposed to do. Like, I’d completely skip the back page, or I’d do the first three steps and then just sort of trail off and start drawing on my folder. It was like, if the teacher was standing right next to my desk, you know, hovering over me or tapping my paper, I could do it. I needed her to literally stay close to me to keep me on track. But the second she walked away to help someone else, my brain would just drift, and I’d miss the second half of the instructions entirely. 

And it's just so frustrating to think about, because I'd always do the homework, or at least start it, but then it would just disappear into the black hole of my backpack and I'd forget to hand it in. People always told me, "You're so smart, if you just applied yourself and paid attention," but I *was* trying! Just like I'm trying with the sanitation logs now! It's like this exact same pattern of just... almost getting there, but leaving the final pieces undone unless someone is standing right over my shoulder watching me do it. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing, it just has much worse consequences now than missing recess did back then.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms of difficulty finishing tasks and trouble starting structured activities, along with a history of similar issues in childhood, are consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation. The lack of depressive symptoms and the specificity of the difficulties to structured tasks at work argue against F33.9 (recurrent depressive disorder) and F43.22 (adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood).

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a lifelong pattern of difficulty initiating and completing tasks, particularly those involving structured routines or checklists, with onset in childhood and persistence into adulthood. The symptoms are specific to structured environments (e.g., school, work) and do not generalize to unstructured or personally motivating tasks. There is no evidence of depressive or anxiety symptoms meeting criteria for other disorders, and the pattern is consistent with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, predominantly inattentive presentation.
